title: The electromagnetic spectrum
examTip: All EM waves travel at 3×10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. Order from lowest to highest frequency: radio → microwave → infrared → visible → UV → X-ray → gamma. Remember: a longer wavelength means a lower frequency.
introTips: All electromagnetic waves are transverse. They all travel at the same speed in a vacuum: 3×10⁸ m/s (300,000,000 m/s).
The only difference between types of EM wave is their frequency, and so their wavelength.
Higher frequency EM waves carry more energy. That is why gamma rays are dangerous and radio waves are not.
A common exam question asks for the use AND the hazard of each wave type.
The visible spectrum is a tiny sliver of the full EM spectrum. Most EM waves are invisible.
intro: Think of your microwave oven and the X-ray machine at the dentist. Think of your phone's Wi-Fi signal and warm sunlight on your skin. These all use different parts of the same thing: the electromagnetic spectrum. EM waves are remarkable because they can travel through a vacuum. That is how sunlight reaches us across 150 million km of empty space. They also all travel at the same speed. What makes radio different from gamma radiation is simply frequency. The spectrum is behind almost every modern communication and medical technology. So it helps to know what each part does and what risks it carries.

keyPoints.heading: What all EM waves have in common
keyPoints.content: All electromagnetic waves are transverse waves. They can travel through a vacuum (empty space) at a speed of 3 × 10⁸ m/s. That is about 300,000,000 m/s, the speed of light. They carry energy and do not need a medium to travel through. The equation v = fλ applies to all EM waves, with v = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. EM waves can be reflected, refracted, diffracted and absorbed. The only difference between types of EM radiation is their frequency, and so their wavelength. The speed is constant. So a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, and the other way round. Higher frequency EM waves carry more energy per photon.

Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = more energy per photon

keyTerms.def: A transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum at 3 × 10⁸ m/s; consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields
3 × 10⁸ m/s — the speed of all EM waves in a vacuum

keyPoints.memTip: All EM waves have the same speed (3×10⁸ m/s), the same type (transverse) and the same equation (v=fλ). A different frequency = a different type.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to think light is faster than radio waves. All EM waves travel at exactly the same speed in a vacuum. Only the frequency differs.

keyPoints.heading: Order of the EM spectrum
keyPoints.content: From lowest to highest frequency (and longest to shortest wavelength): Radio waves → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible light → Ultraviolet → X-rays → Gamma rays. A useful mnemonic: "Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns". Radio waves have the longest wavelengths, up to kilometres. Gamma rays have the shortest, smaller than an atomic nucleus. Visible light is a narrow band in the middle. Within it, red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest. Remember Roy G Biv: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. As you move from radio towards gamma, frequency increases and wavelength decreases. The energy per photon increases too.
writeBullets: Order (low → high frequency): Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, UV, X-ray, Gamma
Mnemonic: 'Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X-ray Guns'
Longer wavelength = lower frequency (because the speed is constant)
Visible spectrum: red (longest λ) → violet (shortest λ). Roy G Biv
Gamma rays have the highest frequency, the shortest wavelength and the most energy

keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise writing the spectrum order from memory in both directions. Exams ask for it both ways.

keyPoints.heading: Uses of each part of the EM spectrum
keyPoints.content: Uses of each type: - Radio waves: broadcasting (TV, radio), long-range communication, MRI scanners. - Microwaves: cooking, satellite communication and mobile phone signals. In cooking, water molecules in food absorb the microwaves, which heats the food. - Infrared (IR): thermal imaging (heat cameras), remote controls (TV remotes), optical fibre communications and night-vision equipment. - Visible light: human vision, photography, cameras and fibre optics. - Ultraviolet (UV): sterilising water and surgical equipment (it kills bacteria), spotting forged banknotes (fluorescent ink), sunbeds and tanning. - X-rays: medical imaging and airport security scanners. In imaging, bones absorb X-rays but soft tissue does not. This makes a shadow image. - Gamma rays: killing cancer cells (radiotherapy), sterilising medical equipment and detecting tumours (PET and gamma scans).

Infrared — thermal imaging, remote controls, optical fibres
Visible — sight, photography, optical fibres
UV — sterilisation, banknote detection, sunbeds

keyTerms.def: EM waves just below visible light in frequency; associated with thermal energy; used in remote controls and thermal cameras

keyPoints.memTip: For each wave type, think of one use you can picture. Radio (music), microwave (oven), IR (TV remote), visible (your eyes), UV (sunbed), X-ray (dentist), gamma (radiotherapy).
keyPoints.tutor_note: Uses often come up in 1–2 mark questions. Learn at least two uses for each wave type.

keyPoints.heading: Hazards of EM radiation
keyPoints.content: Not all EM waves are harmless. The higher the frequency, the more energy per photon. And the more energy, the more damage it can do to living things. - Infrared: too much causes skin burns. It is the heat you feel from fire and sun. - Ultraviolet (UV): damages DNA in skin cells and can cause skin cancer. It damages eyes too, and can cause cataracts. - X-rays: these are ionising radiation. They have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms. This damages DNA and may cause cancer or mutation. Controlled doses are used for medical imaging. - Gamma rays: highly ionising, and the most dangerous type. They cause cancer and cell mutation. They are used in radiotherapy, because when carefully targeted they can also kill cancer cells. Radio, microwave, infrared and visible light are usually thought of as non-ionising. They are safe at normal exposure levels. But too much microwave absorption, or intense IR, can cause heating damage.
writeBullets: Infrared — burns skin if there is too much. Thermal damage
UV — damages DNA. Causes skin cancer and cataracts
X-rays — ionising radiation. DNA damage and cancer risk. Controlled medical doses are low
Gamma — the most ionising. Causes cancer and mutation. Also used to kill cancer cells in radiotherapy
Radio, microwave and visible — usually non-ionising, and safe at normal levels

keyTerms.def: Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, potentially damaging DNA — includes UV, X-rays, and gamma rays
Highest-frequency EM wave; highly ionising; used in cancer treatment (radiotherapy) and sterilisation

keyPoints.memTip: The hazard increases with frequency. IR burns skin, UV causes skin cancer, and X-rays and gamma cause cancer and mutation (ionising). The higher the frequency, the greater the energy and the risk.
keyPoints.tutor_note: People sometimes say X-rays 'see through' the body. In fact, bones absorb X-rays and show up white on the image. Soft tissue lets them pass and shows up dark.

0.question: Which property is the same for all types of electromagnetic wave?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! All EM waves travel at exactly 3 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. Their frequencies and wavelengths differ. That is what makes them different types.
0.wrongFeedback: All EM waves have the same speed in a vacuum: 3 × 10⁸ m/s. What differs is their frequency, and so their wavelength and energy.

1.question: Which part of the EM spectrum is used to sterilise medical equipment and kill cancer cells?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! Gamma rays carry a lot of energy and can kill cells. That makes them dangerous. But it also makes them useful for sterilisation and for targeting tumours in radiotherapy.
1.wrongFeedback: Gamma rays are used for sterilisation and radiotherapy. Their high energy kills bacteria and cancer cells. Radio waves carry far too little energy for this.

3.question: UV radiation is described as a hazard. What is the main risk to the body from too much UV?
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right! UV radiation has enough energy to damage DNA in skin cells. This can trigger mutations that lead to skin cancer. It can also damage the eyes.
3.wrongFeedback: UV radiation damages DNA in skin cells, which can cause skin cancer and cataracts in the eyes. It is ionising enough to break molecular bonds.

commonMistakes: Getting the order of the spectrum wrong. Practise the mnemonic: Radio, Microwave, Infrared, Visible, UV, X-ray, Gamma (low to high frequency).
Saying microwaves cook food by 'vibrating water molecules', without the key detail. Water molecules absorb the microwaves, which transfers energy to them as thermal energy.
Mixing up which way wavelength and frequency go. If frequency increases, wavelength decreases, because the speed is constant: v = fλ.
Saying X-rays 'pass through everything'. Bones absorb X-rays, which is why they look white on X-ray images. It is soft tissue that lets them through.
Forgetting that visible light is part of the EM spectrum too. It is often treated as separate from EM radiation.
examTips: Learn the order of the spectrum in both directions. Questions use 'from lowest to highest frequency' and 'from longest to shortest wavelength'.
For uses and hazards, link the two. Gamma rays are dangerous because they are ionising. But that is exactly why they can kill cancer cells in radiotherapy.
Use v = fλ with v = 3 × 10⁸ m/s for any EM wave calculation.
In 6-mark questions about hazards, always give the frequency comparison to back up your answer. Higher frequency = more energy = more ionising.
For the order of colours within the visible band, remember Roy G Biv: red (lowest frequency) to violet (highest frequency).
